When the Same World Bank Data Can Tell Two Stories

DSC 106 Project 2: Persuasive Visualization
Maxime Chung (mac050@ucsd.edu), Sana Gupta (svgupta@ucsd.edu), Rose Park (sep032@ucsd.edu)
Dataset: World Bank Human Development Indicators, 1960–2020. Indicators used here: GDP per capita, constant 2010 US$ (NY.GDP.PCAP.KD) and life expectancy at birth, total years (SP.DYN.LE00.IN).

Proposition

Higher national income is associated with longer life expectancy, but income alone does not fully explain health outcomes.

This proposition is deliberately arguable from both directions. A country level view shows that countries with similar income can still have meaningfully different life expectancies. A model fitted to all 179 countries shows that income alone explains roughly 70 percent of the cross country variance in life expectancy. The assignment asks us to live inside that tension: not whether one chart is the only true view, but how transformation, framing, and visual emphasis shape what a reader remembers. We argue both halves of the proposition with four visualizations that all draw from the same indicators.

FOR the proposition

Two visualizations emphasize the limits of wealth as an explanation. They keep individual countries visible and quantify the residual variance the model leaves on the table. The headline finding: even granting the income to life expectancy fit, the unexplained 30 percent spans a 20 year gap.

AGAINST the proposition

Two visualizations emphasize how cleanly income organizes life expectancy. The cross sectional fit puts R² at 0.70 with a tight confidence band; the longitudinal panel shows life expectancy rising alongside GDP for sixty years inside every country we plot. The headline framing: wealth and health move together as a rule, not an exception.

Same dataset All four charts draw from the World Bank Human Development Indicators.
Same country universe 179 countries with non null GDP and life expectancy values in 2019.
Same indicators, no jitter GDP per capita constant 2010 US$ on x. Life expectancy at birth on y. Every dot at its true value.

Validation note: this report does not use the earlier buggy Discrepancy in expenditure estimate of GDP column from the checkpoint. The revised pipeline reads the raw indicator files, joins on (Country Name, Year), drops nulls, excludes the source file’s aggregate rows ("World", regional groupings, "OECD members"), and validates against published World Bank values. The chart generation script lives in generate_charts.py alongside the helper module under helpers/.

Scoring scale. Each design decision below is scored on a diverging scale from −2 fully deceptive to +2 fully earnest, in 0.5 steps. The score answers a single question: would a careful reader accept this choice as a defensible reading of the data, or would they say the chart needed their inattention to land? Scores closer to −1 rely on the reader not noticing. Scores closer to +1 survive scrutiny. Scores near 0 are roughly neutral choices.

FOR Visualization 1: income is not destiny

All 179 countries plotted on a linear GDP axis with no fitted curve. Outliers that contradict the wealth equals health intuition are highlighted: Equatorial Guinea, Nigeria, Lesotho, and Eswatini in red (rich for their region but with disappointing life expectancy), and Vietnam, Nicaragua, Honduras, and Bangladesh in green (the opposite). The chart steers the reader to read the cloud as shapeless rather than as a curve.

How to read this chart
  • Each gray dot is one country in 2019 plotted at its true GDP per capita and life expectancy. No jitter.
  • Red highlights: wealthier than the regional average yet shorter lived than predicted.
  • Green highlights: poorer than average yet longer lived than predicted.
  • The x axis is linear. Most countries collapse to a wall on the left, which is part of the persuasive effect.

Design decisions

  1. −1.5
    Linear x axis on GDP per capita deceptive GDP per capita spans almost three orders of magnitude across countries. On a linear axis roughly 90 percent of countries collapse into a vertical wall on the left. The Preston curve, one of the strongest correlations in development economics, becomes invisible. We considered a square root scale as a softer alternative and rejected it because linear was more visually misleading without looking obviously broken.
  2. −1.5
    Cherry picked outlier highlights deceptive The eight highlighted countries are the largest residuals against the trend. Highlighting only outliers pushes the reader to read the chart as no relationship rather than strong relationship with notable exceptions. Showing every country in red or green would have been more honest but less persuasive.
  3. −1
    No fit line, no R² deceptive A regression line fitted on log GDP would yield R² = 0.70 and immediately undercut the chart’s message. Omitting the fit forces the reader to read the cloud by eye, where the linear axis already obscures the relationship. The omission is invisible to a casual reader.
  4. −1.5
    Slanted action title and subtitle deceptive The title "Wealth Is No Cure" and the subtitle "At every income level, health outcomes are all over the map" prime the reader to look for variation rather than trend before they engage with the data. We considered a neutral title ("GDP per capita and life expectancy across 179 countries, 2019") and rejected it as not persuasive enough.
  5. −0.5
    Mild y axis truncation at 50 years mixed The full life expectancy range is roughly 53 to 85 years. Starting the y axis at 50 (rather than 0 or 60) compresses the visible vertical spread slightly, which makes the cloud look more disorderly. The truncation is mild but it is the same family of choice the assignment prompt flags as a typical deceptive move.

FOR Visualization 2: the 20 year gap that wealth does not explain

The FOR side accepts the AGAINST side’s regression line on its own terms, then plots the residuals: how far each country’s actual life expectancy lands from what its GDP per capita predicts. Even granting R² = 0.70, the unexplained 30 percent spans nearly twenty years of life. Equatorial Guinea is sixteen years below its predicted life expectancy. Vietnam is seven above. Wealth alone clearly does not buy health.

How to read this chart
  • The chart uses the AGAINST side’s own log GDP regression to compute one residual per country.
  • Red lollipops: countries that live shorter than the model predicts. Equatorial Guinea is the worst.
  • Green lollipops: countries that live longer than the model predicts. Vietnam is the best.
  • The gray middle band represents 159 other countries the model fits within plus or minus 5 years.

Design decisions

  1. +2
    Use the opposing side’s own regression line as the baseline earnest We did not invent a new model. We took the AGAINST side’s published log GDP fit and plotted what it leaves out. This is steel manning, not strawmanning, and it is the most earnest move in the project. A reader cannot dismiss the chart by saying "your model is wrong" because the model is the opponent’s.
  2. −1
    Show only the top and bottom 10 residuals deceptive The middle 159 countries that the model fits well are compressed into a single gray annotation. This suppresses the visual presence of the 88 percent of countries the model predicts well and elevates the 12 percent it misses. We considered showing all 179 lollipops and rejected it because the chart became unreadable and self defeating.
  3. −0.5
    Diverging red and green palette mixed Red and green carry pre cognitive bad and good associations that load the chart emotionally before the reader processes magnitudes. Mild deception because the encoding is also genuinely informative (negative versus positive residual).
  4. −1.5
    Title frames the unexplained variance as a 20 year gap deceptive The 20 year figure is the actual range from worst to best residual, but the framing converts a statistical residual into a humanitarian indictment. We chose this because residuals alone are emotionally inert.
  5. +1
    Disclose R² = 0.70 in the subtitle earnest The chart explicitly tells the reader that the model the residuals come from explains 70 percent of life expectancy variance. A more deceptive version would have buried this number. Disclosing it makes the chart fall or stand on the interpretation of the unexplained 30 percent.

AGAINST Visualization 1: the strongest pattern in development

The same 179 countries, the same year, the same variables. The only changes from the FOR side’s first chart are the axis scaling, the addition of a fitted regression line with its R², a 95 percent confidence band, five reference countries marked along the curve, and a title that takes the opposite stance.

How to read this chart
  • Same 179 countries. Same 2019 cross section. Same indicators.
  • The x axis is logarithmic. GDP varies across orders of magnitude, so a log scale is the standard encoding.
  • The black line is an OLS fit of life expectancy on log10 of GDP. R² is shown in the legend.
  • The shaded band is the 95 percent confidence interval around the fit.

Design decisions

  1. +1.5
    Logarithmic x axis on GDP per capita earnest GDP per capita is exponential across countries; log is the conventional and expressive encoding. It distributes the points evenly and reveals the underlying Preston curve. Earnest in itself, even though the contrast with the FOR side’s linear axis exposes how much rhetorical weight the axis choice carries.
  2. +1
    Fitted regression line with R² disclosed earnest The fit (life expectancy = 9.9 × log10(GDP) + intercept, R² = 0.70) is shown explicitly in the legend. Plotting the fit and disclosing the R² lets the reader judge how strong the relationship is rather than asking them to estimate it by eye.
  3. +0.5
    95 percent confidence band around the fit mixed The shaded band gives readers an honest sense of the residual spread. The mild deception is that a casual reader may not notice that several countries fall outside the band entirely; the FOR side’s chart 2 makes those countries the whole story.
  4. −1.5
    Slanted action title and subtitle deceptive "The Strongest Pattern in Development" frames a correlation as a near deterministic rule. We chose the language deliberately to mirror the FOR side’s slant. The relationship is real and strong, but the language pushes past what a single year cross section can prove.
  5. −0.5
    Annotate only countries that anchor the trend mixed Five countries (Ethiopia, India, China, United States, Japan) are marked along the curve. They span the full income range and sit close to the fit, which trains the eye to see the chart as a curve rather than as a cloud. Asymmetric attention rather than asymmetric data.

AGAINST Visualization 2: six decades, every country bends the same way

A 2019 cross section is vulnerable to the critique that maybe rich countries just happen to be old. The AGAINST side answers with a longitudinal panel: take six anchor countries that span the full income range (Ethiopia, India, China, South Korea, United States, Japan) and trace life expectancy and GDP per capita from 1960 to 2019. As GDP climbs, life expectancy climbs alongside, in every country we show, for sixty years. Gains range from +9 years (United States) to +33 years (China).

How to read this chart
  • Six panels, one per country. Same y axis (life expectancy, 28 to 88 years) on every panel for honest comparison.
  • The blue line is life expectancy. The gray line is GDP per capita on a logarithmic secondary axis.
  • Each panel carries a green badge with the total life expectancy gain from 1960 to 2019.
  • The country selection is hand picked and shown only six countries; the chart does not show countries whose paths bend the wrong way.

Design decisions

  1. +1
    Same y axis range across all six panels earnest Identical 28 to 88 year limits make magnitudes comparable across countries. Ethiopia’s gain reads as visually as dramatic as China’s. We considered per panel auto scaling and rejected it because it would have flattened Ethiopia and inflated the United States in a way that distorts the actual story.
  2. +1
    Logarithmic GDP on the secondary axis earnest GDP per capita rose by orders of magnitude in some panels (China went from roughly $200 to $8,000). Linear GDP would crush most trajectories into an early flat line. Log is the appropriate encoding for a multiplicative variable.
  3. −2
    Hand picked six countries with strong upward arcs deceptive The most deceptive move on the AGAINST side. Russia in the 1990s, Zimbabwe in the 2000s, Venezuela in the 2010s, and the Soviet collapse would each show life expectancy falling as GDP fell or stagnated. Choosing six poster children turns a real but messy correlation into a triumphal narrative. The title compounds this with "every path."
  4. −1
    Title overclaim: every path bends toward longer life deceptive The chart shows six paths; the title implies all paths. Most readers will not audit the sample. We considered "Six countries" as the title and rejected it as insufficiently emphatic, exactly the kind of choice that the FOR side critiques here.
  5. +0.5
    Annotation showing total life expectancy gain per country mixed Each panel carries an explicit "+9 yrs" or "+33 yrs" badge. The numbers are real and correctly computed. The only slant is that the comparison is across countries that all gained, not against countries that lost.

Reflection

The hardest part of this project was committing to plot the same data on both sides of the cross section. Once we did, the rhetorical machinery became visible. The FOR and AGAINST first charts share every single data point. The proposition flips because of the x axis scale, a fitted curve we drew or did not draw, and a title we wrote. Working in this constraint clarified what counts as a deceptive technique versus a fair editorial choice: a log axis is not deceptive, a linear axis is not deceptive, but choosing one of them while writing a title that depends on the reader not noticing the choice is. The most satisfying chart to build was FOR Visualization 2, which uses the AGAINST side’s own regression line to plot the residuals it leaves behind, because it argues from inside the opponent’s premises rather than swapping them out.

What surprised us was how much of the persuasion lived in things we did not draw. FOR chart 1 is persuasive partly because there is no regression line on it. Adding the same R² = 0.70 line that appears on AGAINST chart 1 would single handedly undo the FOR side’s argument. That asymmetric omission is, in some ways, more dishonest than any positively misleading element of either chart, because nothing on the page would obviously flag it. AGAINST chart 2 was the inverse temptation: hand picking six countries whose trajectories all bent the right way produced a gorgeous, monotonic story that is also the project’s biggest lie of omission. Russia in the 1990s and the post Soviet life expectancy collapse would have made the title false, and we never showed those countries.

Our working definition of ethical visualization is this: a chart is ethical when the reader, given enough time, would still accept the framing (the axes, the fits, the annotations, the country selection, the title) as a defensible reading of the data. A chart is misleading when its persuasive force depends on the reader not having that time. The line we draw between persuasion and deception is the line between framing choices we would defend in public to a critical reader and framing choices that need the reader’s inattention to survive. By that test, FOR Visualization 2 is the most ethical chart in this project (it uses the opponent’s own model and discloses R²), and AGAINST Visualization 2 is the least (it claims "every path" while showing six handpicked ones). All four are persuasive, but they are not equally honest about it.

Methodology and validation

  • Source files: World Bank Human Development Indicators, specifically economy-and-growth.csv and social-development.csv.
  • Indicators: GDP per capita constant 2010 US$ (NY.GDP.PCAP.KD); life expectancy at birth, computed as the unweighted mean of male and female life expectancy from SP.DYN.LE00.MA.IN and SP.DYN.LE00.FE.IN. The World Bank’s population weighted total LE differs by roughly 0.1 years and does not change any conclusion drawn here.
  • Time slice: charts 1 on each side and FOR chart 2 use the 2019 cross section. AGAINST chart 2 extends to a 1960 to 2019 panel for six countries.
  • Country universe: 179 entities for which both indicators are non null in 2019. Aggregate rows ("World", "OECD members", regional groupings) excluded.
  • Joins and nulls: source files contain zero duplicate (Country Name, Year) rows. Inner join on those keys, then drop nulls on both indicators. Identical filter applied to all four charts.
  • Fit: OLS of life expectancy on log10(GDP). Slope = +9.9 years per 10x increase in GDP, R² = 0.70. Reused across AGAINST chart 1 (visualized) and FOR chart 2 (residuals).
  • No jitter: every scatter point sits at its true value. We considered jittering low GDP countries on FOR chart 1 to declutter the left wall and rejected it as undisclosed deception. The crammed left side is the chart’s argument.
  • Subagent assisted design: the second visualization on each side was specced by a data scientist subagent persona (definition sourced from awesome-claude-code-subagents-main/categories/05-data-ai/data-scientist.md), spawned via the Agent tool. The validation pass used the data:validate-data skill: zero duplicate keys, all 12 anchor countries spot checked, R² confirmed at 0.70.
  • SWD chart helpers applied to every render: all four final charts use swd_style(), action_title(), and the check_label_collisions(fix=True) auto fix pass from helpers/chart_helpers.py. The detector resolved 4 collisions on FOR 1, 1 on AGAINST 1, and 0 on the others.
  • Reproducibility: generate_charts.py at the repo root, with helpers under helpers/, regenerates every chart on this page from the source CSVs.
Files in this submission: index.html, images/pro_viz.png, images/pro_viz2.png, images/con_viz.png, images/con_viz2.png, generate_charts.py, helpers/, and PROJECT2_AGENT_CONTEXT.md.
